[p.4] || Kinkade 1993:183: This reduplication looks at first like simple -C2 reduplication because stress most commonly falls on the first vowel of the root; however, enough examples like 'he is going home slowly' occur to indicate that it is location of stress, and not root shape, that determines what is repeated.

new_statements.rule_in_words: No positional rule is given: in underlying (base) forms stress may sit on any vowel, so its position must be lexically specified; it most often lands on the first vowel of the root. Surface position is then adjusted by vowel deletion: when the stressed vowel before a single final consonant is deleted in the unpossessed noun, stress moves leftward to the next vowel; unstressed vowels before CCV are deleted and unstressed *a reduces to schwa, so stress and vowel quality co-vary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either paper. Kinkade 1993 (p. 197) notes that Upper Chehalis compounds are one phonological unit with a single primary stress; no statement for Cowlitz.
new_statements.exceptions: 1971 paper lists residues: 35 nouns (some recent polysyllabic loans) that fail to drop the pre-final vowel or shift stress, and forms with irregular possessive allomorphs -hi/-ni/-(i)li that likewise keep stem vowel and stress; two forms with 'unexplained stress shifts'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: noun stems, independent (citation) vs. third-person possessed forms elicited from two speakers (Emma Mesplie, Lucy James); 1993 remarks concern Cowlitz and Upper Chehalis jointly and the illustrative reduplication examples are Upper Chehalis. Neither source is a dedicated phonology/stress section; Kinkade 2004 grammatical sketch (unseen) is the authoritative description and should supersede.
new_statements.identity_note: Cowlitz here = Lower Cowlitz Salish (ƛʼpúlmixq), glottocode cowl1242, Inland Tsamosan; all data trace to Kinkade's 1960s fieldwork with Emma Mesplie and Lucy James. The 'Upper Cowlitz' (Taidnapam) spoke Sahaptin, not this language. Kinkade 1993's stress remarks are made for Cowlitz and Upper Chehalis (uppe1275) together and the illustrative forms on p. 183 are Upper Chehalis.

sources.note: Morphophonology of noun stems: base forms CVC/(X)CV(X)CC/(X)CV(X)CVC and 'Stress may fall on any vowel' (p.3); Rule 2 deletes the vowel before a single final consonant and if that vowel was stressed 'stress is shifted to the next vowel toward the beginning of the word' (p.4); Rule 4 deletes unstressed vowels before CCV (p.4); *a surfaces as a only if stressed, else unstressed schwa (p.6).

sources.note: Cowlitz and Upper Chehalis keep/lose underlying vowels by open vs closed syllable, not by stress as elsewhere in Salish (p.178); stress-oriented -C2 reduplication in Cowlitz and Upper Chehalis 'because stress most commonly falls on the first vowel of the root.. it is location of stress, and not root shape, that determines what is repeated' (p.183, examples Upper Chehalis); Cowlitz and Upper Chehalis form diminutives by lengthening the stressed vowel (p.189); long vowel = length plus sharp pitch drop and creakiness (p.179); compounds carry a single primary stress (Upper Chehalis, p.197).
